working_title: He Lived 60 Hours at the Bottom of the Sea
alt_title: The Cook Who Breathed in a Sunken Ship
subject: Harrison Okene, cook on the tug Jascon-4, capsized off Nigeria on 26 May 2013. He survived ~60 h in an air pocket (~4 ft high) at ~30 m until DCN divers, sent to recover bodies, found him on 28 May. He then spent ~60 h in decompression. 11 crew died.
why_potential: It has a single impossible number (60 hours), a shrinking-air clock, and a twist (the divers were recovering bodies). The air-pocket physics suits animation. The real rescue footage went viral globally in Dec 2013, so recognition is proven. It is evergreen survival content.

working_title: 30 Minutes With No Air, 100 m Down
alt_title: The Diver Who Should Be Dead
subject: Chris Lemons, saturation diver on DSV Bibby Topaz, North Sea, 18 Sep 2012. A dynamic-positioning failure severed his umbilical at ~90-100 m. He had ~5-10 min of bailout gas, was found unresponsive and revived in the bell by Duncan Allcock with Dave Yuasa. Reported times without main supply vary from ~20 to ~40 min. Documentary Last Breath (2019); feature film (2025).
why_potential: An impossible-survival anchor plus a medical mystery (cold and high-O2 bailout are reported hypotheses). Thoughty2 1.2M; the trailer reportedly 7.8M; a 2025 film keeps it topical.

working_title: Why Divers Fear the Arch
alt_title: The Red Sea's Most Dangerous Dive Site
subject: The Blue Hole, Dahab, Egypt: a marine sinkhole beside a reef wall with a tunnel called 'the Arch' at ~55 m (181 ft) - beyond recreational air limits. A memorial wall of plaques on shore commemorates dozens of divers, mostly lost attempting the Arch on air, many from nitrogen narcosis. Egyptian authorities publish no official death toll. Yuri Lipski (2000) is the best-known case; freediver Stephen Keenan died there in 2017 (Netflix 'The Deepest Breath'). Framed as a site-safety explainer.
why_potential: Proven 'killer dive site' demand (MrBallen 5.6M on a different blue hole; Netflix 'The Deepest Breath'). The science of narcosis is visual. Ethics sharply limit the human story, so feasibility of a respectful version is fine, but story score is capped.

working_title: Found 5.5 km Down, 72 Years Later
alt_title: The Ship That Delivered the Bomb
subject: USS Indianapolis (CA-35) delivered atomic-bomb components to Tinian, then was torpedoed by Japanese submarine I-58 shortly after midnight on 30 Jul 1945 (sinking time 00:14 per NHHC). Of ~1,195 crew, roughly 800-900 went into the water; 316 survived after days adrift (exposure, dehydration, sharks). In 2016 NHHC historian Richard Hulver found that tank landing ship LST-779 had logged passing the cruiser ~11 h before it sank - shifting the search area west. Paul Allen's R/V Petrel found the wreck on 19 Aug 2017 at ~5,500 m (18,000 ft) in the Philippine Sea. Location kept secret; war grave.
why_potential: A deep-sea discovery with an infamous survival story, plus a perfect detective beat: a forgotten deck log of a passing landing ship cracked a 72-year mystery. Demand is high, but the deaths are sensitive and the sharks are heavily covered. Smithsonian's 4.4K shows that packaging matters.

working_title: A Whole Fleet Is Still Down There

subject: Chuuk (Truk) Lagoon, Micronesia: US carrier raid Operation Hailstone (17-18 Feb 1944) destroyed roughly 250+ Japanese aircraft and sank dozens of ships (estimates range from ~40 to ~70 vessels by source). It is now a world-famous wreck-diving site, with holds still holding aircraft and vehicles. Shinkoku Maru and Yamagiri Maru are well-known dives (~9-37 m). Cousteau's 1969 documentary popularised it. 30 US aircraft were lost.
why_potential: The scale reveal ('an entire fleet') plus cargo still in the holds. Wreck exploration is highly feasible procedurally. Moderate demand; there is no single protagonist, so the story is weaker.

working_title: 16 Years of 'Today's the Day'
alt_title: The Treasure That Cost Him His Son
subject: Treasure hunter Mel Fisher searched from 1969 for the Spanish galleon Nuestra Señora de Atocha (sank in a 1622 hurricane off the Florida Keys) under the motto 'Today's the day'. On 20 Jul 1975 the salvage boat Northwind capsized at night, killing his son Dirk, Dirk's wife Angel and diver Rick Gage. Exactly ten years later, on 20 Jul 1985, son Kane radioed that they had found the 'mother lode' (estimated ~$400-450 million). His company won a long legal fight over the treasure (Supreme Court 1982, reported).
why_potential: Obsession, tragedy and payoff, with a built-in catchphrase loop and an eerie same-date coincidence (20 July 1975 / 20 July 1985). Treasure is a strong click driver. Wreck and gold piles are feasible.

working_title: They Nuked a Fleet, and You Can Dive It
alt_title: Atomic Ghost Fleet
subject: Bikini Atoll, Marshall Islands: Operation Crossroads (1946) - Test Able (1 Jul, air burst) and Test Baker (25 Jul, underwater) against a target fleet. The carrier USS Saratoga sank after Baker; the Japanese battleship Nagato sank days later (29 Jul) and lies upside down. About 21 Crossroads wrecks are diveable at Bikini and Kwajalein (advanced/technical diving only). The Bikinians were relocated and contamination still prevents permanent return. 'Bikini Atoll Nuclear Test Site' was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2010.
why_potential: An extreme juxtaposition (atom bomb plus coral) and an aircraft carrier you can swim into. Moderate demand. The displacement of the Bikinians must be mentioned respectfully.

working_title: The 'Mount Everest' of Wreck Diving
alt_title: The Luxury Liner That Keeps Claiming Divers
subject: SS Andrea Doria, Italian liner, collided with MS Stockholm in fog off Nantucket on the night of 25 Jul 1956 and sank the next morning; 46 died on Andrea Doria and 5 on Stockholm, while most of the ~1,706 aboard were rescued. Fog, speed and misuse of radar were cited as contributing causes. The wreck (~240-250 ft / ~76 m) was dubbed the 'Mount Everest of wreck diving' (credited to cameraman Al Giddings); reported diver deaths range from ~16 to 18+.
why_potential: A fog collision with radar confusion is a good mid-turn. 'Most dangerous wreck' framing. Lower name recognition with younger audiences.

alt_title: Baltic Sea 'UFO'
subject: In 2011 the Swedish Ocean X team's side-scan sonar showed a ~60 m circular object at ~90 m in the Gulf of Bothnia. The team CLAIMED electronics failed near it. Geologists who examined samples say it is a natural glacial deposit. CLAIM vs CONSENSUS.

working_title: Why Is There a Statue of Jesus 17 m Underwater?
alt_title: Christ of the Abyss
subject: Il Cristo degli Abissi, a 2.5 m bronze by Guido Galletti, placed on 22 Aug 1954 at ~17 m (some sources say 18 m) in San Fruttuoso bay near Camogli, Italy. Idea credited to diving instructor Duilio Marcante; commemorates diver Dario Gonzatti (reported died 1947) and others lost at sea. Copies exist elsewhere (e.g., Key Largo).
why_potential: A strange-image curiosity gap with a heartfelt memorial answer. Low demand and low stakes, but very feasible and calm. Useful as a gentle, loopable Short.
